n: A new section of Isaiah begins with tenderness. After warning of exile to Babylon (chapter 39), the Lord looks ahead to His captive people and says, twice for emphasis, “Comfort My people.” Many scholars think chapters 40–66 address the exiles; Latter-day Saints accept them as Isaiah’s prophetic words.

f.w: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people
f.g: The doubled command shows urgency and deep compassion.

n: Speak to Jerusalem’s heart: her hard service is over, her sin is forgiven. “Double” may mean she has suffered fully, or that God’s pardon now matches her suffering in full measure.

f.g: Literally “speak to the heart”—tender, persuasive words.
Hebrew tsaba—hard service or term of enlistment, here the time of exile.

n: A herald calls out to build a road through the desert for the Lord, as servants prepared roads for a king’s arrival. All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus.

f.w: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness
Prepare ye the way of the LORD

n: Valleys raised, mountains leveled, crooked paths straightened—a picture of removing every obstacle. Spiritually, it suggests preparing hearts by humbling the proud and lifting the lowly.
When the way is ready, the Lord’s glory will be revealed and all people will see it together. Latter-day Saints also see a future fulfillment at the Second Coming.

f.w: all flesh shall see it together

n: A voice tells the prophet to cry out; he asks what message to give. The answer: human beings are like grass and wildflowers—beautiful but brief.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed here—beauty, constancy, or loyalty; human faithfulness doesn’t last.

n: Grass dries up when the hot desert wind blows. So human life and power fade quickly under God’s breath.

f.g: Hebrew ruach—breath or wind; the scorching east wind that withers plants.

n: The contrast that matters: people fade, but God’s word stands forever. His promises of comfort and redemption can be trusted.

f.w: the word of our God shall stand for ever

n: Zion is told to climb a high mountain and shout the good news without fear: “Here is your God!” This is gospel language—the joyful announcement that God is coming to save.

f.g: The Greek Old Testament uses the word family behind “gospel” (euangelion) here.

n: The Lord comes as a mighty ruler, His arm representing His power. He brings His reward with Him—the people He has redeemed, and justice for all.
The same powerful King is also a gentle Shepherd: He gathers lambs in His arms, carries them close, and leads nursing ewes carefully. Jesus later called Himself the Good Shepherd.

f.w: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd

n: A series of questions shows God’s greatness: who can hold the oceans in a palm, measure the sky with a hand’s width, and weigh mountains on a scale? Only the Creator.

f.g: The distance from thumb to little finger with the hand spread—about 9 inches.

n: No one advised God or gave Him directions. He needs no counselor.

f.w: Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD

n: The questions continue: from whom did God learn justice or wisdom? The implied answer is no one—He is the source of all understanding.

f.g: The way of justice, right order.

n: Compared to God, the great nations are like a drop falling from a bucket or a speck of dust on a scale—too small to matter in the weighing.

f.g: Coastlands and islands—distant lands, often around the Mediterranean.

n: Even all of Lebanon’s forests as firewood and its animals as offerings would not be enough sacrifice to honor God properly.
Before God all nations are as nothing. This is not contempt for people but a reminder that no empire can rival Him.
So to whom could God be compared? The question sets up a satire of idol-making.

f.w: To whom then will ye liken God

n: A craftsman casts an idol, a goldsmith covers it in gold and adds silver chains. The “god” is entirely a human product.
A poor man who can’t afford gold picks wood that won’t rot and hires a skilled carpenter so his idol won’t topple over. Isaiah’s irony: a god that has to be kept from falling down.

f.g: An offering; here the costly material for an idol.

n: Haven’t you known this from the very beginning? Creation itself testifies who God is.

f.w: from the foundations of the earth

n: God sits enthroned above the earth’s horizon; people look like grasshoppers from there. He spreads the sky like a tent curtain for people to live under.

f.g: The vault or horizon; Hebrew ḥug, the circle of sky over the earth.

f.w: stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain

n: He can bring the most powerful rulers to nothing.
Proud rulers are like seedlings that barely take root—one breath from God and they wither and blow away like straw.

f.g: The dry stalks left after harvest.

n: The Holy One Himself repeats the challenge: is anyone equal to Me?
Look at the stars: God created them, leads them out like an army in order, and calls each by name. Not one is missing. If He knows every star, He knows each of us.

f.w: he calleth them all by names

n: God addresses discouraged Israel, who complain that He doesn’t see their trouble or care about their rights. Many exiles likely felt forgotten.

f.w: My way is hid from the LORD

n: The answer: the eternal God, Creator of the whole earth, never gets tired, and His understanding is beyond measure. He hasn’t lost track of you.
He gives strength to the worn out and power to the powerless.

f.w: He giveth power to the faint

n: Even young, fit people get exhausted and stumble. Human strength alone isn’t enough.

But those who wait on the Lord—trusting and hoping in Him—gain new strength. They soar like eagles, run without weariness, and walk without fainting. The Word of Wisdom promise in D&C 89 echoes this verse.

f.g: Hebrew qavah—to wait with hopeful expectation, like a cord being twisted tight.

f.w: they shall run, and not be weary
